📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A near-record share of young adults won’t be traveling home to visit family for the holidays—they’re already living there. One in three U.S. adults between age 18 and 34 live with their parents, according to a latest report from Realtor.com. That’s 25.2 million or 33% of young adults living at home in 2025, only a sliver less than the 33.6% during the pandemic-era peak in 2020. Living at home is one way that Americans who can’t afford to buy or rent on their own wrestle with the high cost of housing and other expenses. While the cost of housing is a nationwide problem, the share of adults living with their parents offers an interesting glimpse into regional affordability patterns around the country. “The pattern of young adults at home has spread beyond the most expensive markets, with the share rising most in parts of the South and West, including some that have traditionally supported an earlier launch,” Realtor.com’s chief economist, Danielle Hale, wrote in the report. “As young people adapt to high housing costs, they are delaying homeownership and the wealth creation that comes with it.” Two stories with the same ending Predictably, at least one of the country’s priciest cities is among those with the largest share of adults living with their parents—but the full story is more complicated. New York leads the list, with 41.3% of adults between the ages of 18 and 24 staying in the nest. In Philadelphia, Miami, Baltimore, and Houston, more than 38% of adults in that age range lived with their parents. Across Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Chicago, the share of adults living at home was over 35%. Houston, Atlanta, and Baltimore aren’t known for their high cost of living, unlike costly urban hubs like New York and Los Angeles, but home prices have soared in recent years in those markets. That rapid change to local affordability is freezing many young adults out of a housing market they might have been able to afford during a previous era. The share of adults living at home has grown the quickest in Las Vegas, San Francisco, and San Jose, but those metros tell different stories. In San Francisco and San Jose, two expensive cities close to the AI boom, housing prices have always been high, even as they grow higher still. In Las Vegas, once known as a relatively affordable market in the West, home prices have skyrocketed by more than 60% since 2019. “Las Vegas and the Bay Area show two different paths to the same challenge,” wrote Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com. “In Las Vegas, the sharp rise in home prices has made it harder for young adults to buy. In San Francisco and San Jose, already-high housing costs and limited inventory leave many young adults facing steep barriers to living on their own.” Living at home on the rise Regionally, the Northeast still dominates with 36.9% of young adults living at home in 2025, though that number is trending down. The West is next with a 32.4% “co-residence” rate, followed by 32.3% in the South and 31.7% in the Midwest. That share is rising everywhere except the Northeast, demonstrating that the housing affordability crisis may look distinct in different corners of the country, but it’s something that a surprising share of Americans everywhere are struggling with. “For young adults who hope to live independently or buy a home, elevated costs and limited entry-level supply can delay household formation and, for would-be buyers, the opportunity to build home equity,” Jones said. “Until affordability improves and entry-level supply expands, the report finds that pent-up demand is likely to continue accumulating.”.

Recent findings suggest that friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

According to recent reports, in this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge showed up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Recent findings suggest that either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

Industry observers note that it's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:.

It has been revealed that most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Recent findings suggest that log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

In a recent development, most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

Mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

Two storage rules save you pain later:.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:.

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:.

The psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

Sources indicate that for digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Sources indicate that use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:.

Sources indicate that store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

In a recent development, keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Industry observers note that yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

Sources indicate that the pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:.

Recent findings suggest that the verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

In a recent development, the hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only highlights how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

Chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:.

The tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

On top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:.

Industry observers note that that evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

According to recent reports, card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

In a recent development, the threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:.

If you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

According to recent reports, PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:.

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code problems the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

It has been revealed that then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:.

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Industry observers note that don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

It has been revealed that if you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

According to recent reports, mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

According to recent reports, no. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Sources indicate that yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Industry News: Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions.
  • Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs.
  • Sources indicate that the proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-released uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this new component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).

Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.

Sources indicate that the proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.

It has been revealed that these laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco firm’s chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship.
  • It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company’s chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship.
  • Sources indicate that will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?There’s reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute’s Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have “actually managed to empty the safe” is low.The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco firm’s chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing “this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good.”“We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse,” Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained newly introduced steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record $1.5 trillion valuation. The Claude AI tool maker already prepares to dedicate 5% of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they’ll give away 80% of their equity — a $112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves — riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading U.S. AI firms’ valuations could add at least $37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.“This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty,” mentioned Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.Nonprofits aren’t counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. The sector’s volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.“The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard,” said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. “That’s not an automatic step.” AI philanthropists are expected to make large donations swiftly Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?There’s reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute’s Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have “actually managed to empty the safe” is low.The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation rolled out to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of “extreme peril” and “really transformative promise” that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.At least one of Anthropic’s co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children’s savings program, according to comments made Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.Anthropic’s explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving program adds another incentive. Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.“The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already,” Nash said. “And they are giving now, right?” Tech-adjacent nonprofits prepare for influx One organization in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than $8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to $1 billion.The move reflected expectations of “considerably more future funding for this kind of work,” according to the announcement.“We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends,” Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. “But there is a great deal of room for other organizations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role.”GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about $15, usually subtracted from recipients’ first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.“I have this level of cautious optimism,” Allardice said. “But I can’t foresee the future, and I don’t know exactly what’s going to happen.”Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It’s the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritizes donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.The movement’s reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects “quite a bit” of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more vital, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors’ giving.“As you can imagine, it’s a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon,” Shorb said. “As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we’ve tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach.” Associated Press coverage of philanthropy and nonprofits receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content. For all of AP’s philanthropy coverage, visit https://apnews.com/hub/philanthropy. —James Pollard, Associated Press.

The free market isn’t so free. Just look at Jensen Huang

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s plenty to scratch your head about in the speedy and surprising return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, just 11 days after he resigned following revelations of an affair with a woman who may have helped make him a target of Chinese intelligence.
  • Sources indicate that there’s plenty to scratch your head about in the speedy and surprising return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, just 11 days after he resigned following revelations of an affair with a woman who may have helped make him a target of Chinese intelligence.
  • It has been revealed that perhaps most head-scratching of all is the White House’s claim to reporters that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang’s return to the manufacturer, and reports that he dialed into a board meeting to argue for the return of the executive whose resignation the board had accepted less than two weeks earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s plenty to scratch your head about in the speedy and surprising return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, just 11 days after he resigned following revelations of an affair with a woman who may have helped make him a target of Chinese intelligence. Never mind the fact that two other allegations of improper relationships with Nvidia employees have emerged, alongside a slew of claims about his reportedly toxic management style. Or that he’s still, technically, under investigation, according to Nvidia’s statement announcing his return. Or that six days earlier, the board told investors it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Perhaps most head-scratching of all is the White House’s claim to reporters that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang’s return to the company, and reports that he dialed into a board meeting to argue for the return of the executive whose resignation the board had accepted less than two weeks earlier. Trump has since claimed in a call to CNBC following the announcement that Huang was “exonerated”—before adding, almost incongruously, that “he’s in the business of selling chips.” (That leap between one thought—the basis for which remains unclear, given the unfinished independent investigation—and another tells its own story.) Senator Elizabeth Warren has called the decision “reckless.” There’s another word for it that might come to mind. But the most diplomatic way to say it is that it’s the end of a free market in the United States. Leaders of countries can have their own opinions about who should run a major company operating in their country. But they shouldn’t be influencing boardroom discussions about the running of that company. Nvidia’s own announcement acknowledges that directors received “input from senior levels” of the U.S. government before concluding that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk. The massive losses in the stock market, with Nvidia a lynchpin of the AI boom, won’t have gone unnoticed at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. And for a man who professes to be the master of “the art of the deal,” a deal that boosted Nvidia’s market value by roughly $1 trillion in a matter of hours sounds like a pretty sweet deal. But rising share prices don’t answer questions about Huang’s conduct, or his paramour’s potential ties to Chinese intelligence. Nor do they explain why a supposedly independent board tasked with holding executives accountable appears to have allowed a world leader to influence its deliberations and ultimately sway its decision. Trump, after all, explicitly said he “convinced them” to reinstate Huang. And what about the Nvidia employees on the receiving end of Huang’s reported tirades? According to The Fresh York Times, he has threatened to rip off employees’ arms and beat them to death with them, tear the tops of their heads off and “pee on your brain,” and told one employee that his mother should have aborted him. To be sure, many Nvidia employees have expressed support for Huang. But at least when Sam Altman was deposed as CEO by his board at OpenAI nearly three years ago to the day, the groundswell of opinion in favor of reinstating him represented a near-unanimous employee revolt. The truth is that Jensen Huang may ultimately be cleared of the most serious allegations being made against him—that’s literally what investigations are for. But the independent investigation hasn’t concluded. And some of the most powerful people in America seem to have arrived at the verdict first, and decided the process can catch up later. That’s not a free market. But it is a significant, beautiful trade.

Or that he’s still, technically, under investigation, according to Nvidia’s statement announcing his return. Or that six days earlier, the board told investors it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”.

It has been revealed that perhaps most head-scratching of all is the White House’s claim to reporters that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang’s return to the manufacturer, and reports that he dialed into a board meeting to argue for the return of the executive whose resignation the board had accepted less than two weeks earlier. Trump has since claimed in a call to CNBC following the announcement that Huang was “exonerated”—before adding, almost incongruously, that “he’s in the business of selling chips.” (That leap between one thought—the basis for which remains unclear, given the unfinished independent investigation—and another tells its own story.).

Sources indicate that senator Elizabeth Warren has called the decision “reckless.” There’s another word for it that might come to mind. But the most diplomatic way to say it is that it’s the end of a free market in the United States.

Leaders of countries can have their own opinions about who should run a major company operating in their country. But they shouldn’t be influencing boardroom discussions about the running of that company. Nvidia’s own announcement acknowledges that directors received “input from senior levels” of the U.S. government before concluding that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk.

The massive losses in the stock market, with Nvidia a lynchpin of the AI boom, won’t have gone unnoticed at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. And for a man who professes to be the master of “the art of the deal,” a deal that boosted Nvidia’s market value by roughly $1 trillion in a matter of hours sounds like a pretty sweet deal.

But rising share prices don’t answer questions about Huang’s conduct, or his paramour’s potential ties to Chinese intelligence. Nor do they explain why a supposedly independent board tasked with holding executives accountable appears to have allowed a world leader to influence its deliberations and ultimately sway its decision. Trump, after all, explicitly mentioned he “convinced them” to reinstate Huang.

Industry observers note that and what about the Nvidia employees on the receiving end of Huang’s reported tirades? According to The Newly introduced York Times, he has threatened to rip off employees’ arms and beat them to death with them, tear the tops of their heads off and “pee on your brain,” and told one employee that his mother should have aborted him. To be sure, many Nvidia employees have expressed support for Huang. But at least when Sam Altman was deposed as CEO by his board at OpenAI nearly three years ago to the day, the groundswell of opinion in favor of reinstating him represented a near-unanimous employee revolt.

In a recent development, the truth is that Jensen Huang may ultimately be cleared of the most serious allegations being made against him—that’s literally what investigations are for. But the independent investigation hasn’t concluded. And some of the most powerful people in America seem to have arrived at the verdict first, and decided the process can catch up later. That’s not a free market. But it is a big, beautiful trade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC Spain has kicked off a latest marketing campaign that leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026, gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release, folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray-style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and a redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.

Sources indicate that 'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.

Industry observers note that the KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.

GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games mentioned. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media-friendly way.

KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef with ROG branding.

#104455. Does culture change people’s personalities?

Does culture change people’s personalities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that personality is often misunderstood.
  • Industry observers note that personality is often misunderstood.
  • It has been revealed that and yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that personality is often misunderstood. For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. In fact, everybody has a preferred pattern of reactions to different situations, and if you hang out with people long enough you will have no trouble predicting how they are likely to act in any given situation, or indeed understanding what makes them tick. And yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation. One of the earliest findings in psychology is that behavior is always a function of both the person and the situation, which means that in order to predict how people will act you must take into account not just who they are but also what the situational requirements are. Micro vs. Macro At the micro-level, this explains why personality may be “suppressed” or inhibited in strong situations, that is contexts where there is a great deal of pressure to behave in a specific way or form: from a church (quiet, respectful, pensative) to a nightclub (loud, extraverted, energetic), to a lecture (focused, pensative, attentive), to a soccer game (depending on where you are, anywhere from excited and energized to aggressive and stressed). That is not to say that people stop being who they are when they are required to inhibit their personality; but rather, that personality becomes a weaker predictor of behavior when the strength of the situation temporarily eclipses it. At the macro-level, this begs the question of how much our personality may change when we make substantial long-term changes in our chosen environments or contexts. Most notably, people changing jobs or employers will often switch from one organizational culture to another; and people switching cities or countries will also be faced with different cultural demands to adapt or adjust their behaviors. Let me use myself as an example: moving from Argentina to Britain first, then from Britain to the US, required shaping my main adaptations to meet the cultural demands of each environment: I first learned to become less excitable, emotional, and direct (all of which work far less in Britain than Argentina), and then learned to suppress the sarcasm, nuances and indirectness in my communication (as these are less effective in the US than Britain). But, what does the research show about how culture, either at the societal or organizational level, impacts people’s behavior? And can this impact be significant or consequential enough to translate into actual personality changes? Adaptations Let’s start with the second question, which is actually simpler. Since personality can mostly be understood as “what you typically or habitually do,” enduring changes to how you behave—fresh adaptations—will indeed be perceived as personality changes. So, for instance, after living in NYC for over a decade the fast-paced nature of the city can make you more impatient, to a point that may not make you stand out in NYC (where type-A impatience is the norm) but will certainly stand out if you transfer that impactience to slower tempo cultures. As the famous line suggests, “The problem with city people in the countryside is that they expect even nature to meet deadlines.” Note, however, that city people often come from the countryside in the first place, but unless they adapt to their new fast environments and adopt the appropriate speed, they will not last very long. As for the first question, there’s plenty of research evidence—especially recent scientific papers—showing that while the essence of personality may remain largely unchanged even after people switch cultures, there are still logical changes to their personality at the more granular level, which correspond to the adaptational requirements of their adoptive cultures. In a way, we could say that our personality evolves when we go outside our comfort zone and challenge ourselves with new contexts that require new adaptations and broadening the behavioral repertoire in our tool kit. For example, a recent longitudinal study comparing 300 Japanese students studying in the United States with 108 students who remained in Japan found that international experiences were associated with changes in personality-related behaviors, particularly greater openness to new experiences and more socially adaptive behavior. Interestingly, the researchers also found that students who chose to study abroad already differed from those who stayed home, suggesting that personality not only influences how we adapt to new environments, but also which environments we choose to enter in the first place. Likewise, a recent meta-analysis examining 25 studies, comprising 40 samples and over 5,700 participants, found that living and studying abroad was associated with measurable personality changes, including increased openness to experience, greater self-confidence and agency, and lower levels of neuroticism (that is, greater emotional stability). Although the effects were generally small, the findings suggest that personality is not simply something we carry with us wherever we go, but also something that is shaped by the environments and cultures we inhabit. In another longitudinal study tracking 180 British university students, some of whom spent a year abroad across 32 different destinations, those living overseas became somewhat more agreeable, curious, and less anxious than their peers who remained at home. Interestingly, although the overall personality changes were relatively small, the researchers found that people’s everyday behavioral tendencies predicted longer-term personality change, suggesting that adapting how we behave in unfamiliar environments may eventually influence who we become. Perhaps even more intriguingly, a series of four studies examining Spanish-English bilinguals found that people’s reported personality characteristics varied depending on the language they were using. Specifically, participants tended to report higher levels of extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness when responding in English rather than Spanish, consistent with the cultural norms associated with each language. This suggests that our personality is not always expressed in the same way across situations, and that simply switching languages may activate different aspects of our identity, even without changing countries. Workplace influence Even career or employment switches can shape people’s personality, as a growing body of research suggests that our jobs are not just an expression of who we are, but can also influence who we become. For example, a longitudinal study tracking Australian workers over five years found that moving into more senior managerial and professional roles was associated with increases in openness to experience, while another study examining nearly 7,700 German workers found that occupational demands were associated with subsequent personality development, particularly among those who remained in their jobs long enough to be shaped by them. Likewise, a longitudinal study following people from age 18 to 26 found that work experiences and personality influenced each other, such that people tended to select jobs compatible with their existing traits, but those same jobs subsequently reinforced or modified their personalities. In other words, we may choose our careers based on our personalities, but our careers can also end up choosing the personalities we develop. Of all these patterns of change, the most salient is the positive impact that environmental and cultural switches have on openness to experience, the academic term for intellectual and experiential curiosity. Interestingly, the effect is a form of “snowballing” whereby cultures operate in a way that accentuate who people are in the first place. In other words, our choices are a function of our inherent or a priori preferences and dispositions, and they contribute to augmenting them. This is why when people change, the most common outcome is that they become a more exaggerated version of their earlier selves. Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of niche-picking, whereby people gravitate towards environments, relationships, and experiences that are compatible with their existing personalities. Importantly, this is not just a matter of selecting environments that suit us, but also being shaped by them, as illustrated by a longitudinal study showing that the personality traits that predispose people to certain work experiences tend to be reinforced by those same experiences over time. In other words, curious people may seek intellectually stimulating environments that make them even more curious, while competitive individuals may gravitate towards demanding, high-pressure cultures that further amplify their competitiveness. Thus, we don’t just choose environments that reflect who we are; we also become more like the environments we choose. Paradoxically, then, the more we change, the more we become like ourselves.

#104454. Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2530 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
  • Recent findings suggest that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
  • According to recent reports, that’s very worrying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing. Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy. That’s very worrying. The people designing these tools and running these companies decide what the technology is for, whose tasks get automated, and how the value is captured. If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that. But after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see. I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership demonstrates women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. But do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in which many women leaders from across the globe had talked about AI from another angle: regulating it, contesting it, limiting its costs for communities and the environment. These women show that many are involved in initiatives shaping the future of AI. A narrow definition of AI work The first blind spot is in the definition. LinkedIn counts someone as “AI talent” if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills. There may be a will to also count “implied skills”, i.e. for people in occupations that assume AI expertise even if they haven’t tagged it on their profile, but by and large the lens remains mainly technical. Women’s share of C-suite roles held by AI talent at AI companies is remarked to be 13%. But it leaves out government and civil society as well as leaders within the AI industry who don’t hold technical titles. Skills raise the same question. LinkedIn separates AI literacy, meaning the use of tools like ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot, from the engineering skills needed to build the technology. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she didn’t know whether it is counted at all, “because it’s not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool that you would be using.” We have seen this before. The previous generation of tech jobs was measured with coding as the yardstick, and women who ran product, policy, or trust and safety teams barely demonstrated up in the count. Decisions made from the outside If leadership means making decisions that change the course of AI, many of those decisions are now made outside AI companies. On Nov. 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all of which aimed at limiting construction. Voters approved nearly all of them. And women are prominent in these fights. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George’s County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum’s petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project. In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June. The revolt is likely to change the industry. It is “forcing a lot of AI leaders to have to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public,” Steinberg said. When companies arrive in towns and ask local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements, on the assumption that residents would welcome a transformative technology, “what they’re finding is that the benefits that people are experiencing from this technology are not outweighing the negatives that having a data center in their community would present,” she added. Data centers do create some jobs, she added, but “whether that is at a level that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide.” Europe tells a similar story. Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU’s work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office. In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50 % of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules. It’s true that some of the best-known critics of the industry, like Timnit Gebru, did not choose to stand outside the AI industry: they were pushed out. Women end up regulating and contesting AI because public-sector, legal, and community careers are more inclusive, while the best-paid technical jobs remain largely in the hands of tech bros who perpetuate a culture that actively filters women out. The women we miss Another blind spot is usage: women may use AI more than they admit. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code. When told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price: a 13% drop in perceived competence, compared with 6% for men. Because of this “hidden penalty of using AI”, any measure of AI skills based on self-reporting is likely to miss all the women who choose not to mention their use and their skills. Steinberg also pointed to the skills employers now want. Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation, conflict management. She is bullish on women’s strengths there, but she warned that “we haven’t really figured out the code” to train, evaluate, and promote people on those skills. Until we do, that contribution will remain mostly invisible too. The case for counting differently None of this is an argument for complacency. Women should be building AI tools and running AI companies, where decisions about capital and products are made. A 13% share of C-suite AI leadership roles is a disaster. And LinkedIn’s data can help better fight this fight. Because it tracks how people move from job to job, it shows where women drop off, and the answer varies by industry. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite. Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level. In STEM, it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job. But a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation, and everyday use. If we could map the gap across industry, government, and civil society, we would have a better baseline, and it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest.

Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy.

If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that.

According to recent reports, but after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see.

It has been revealed that I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership shows women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills.

Recent findings suggest that but do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in which many women leaders from across the globe had talked about AI from another angle: regulating it, contesting it, limiting its costs for communities and the environment. These women show that many are involved in initiatives shaping the future of AI.

The first blind spot is in the definition. LinkedIn counts someone as “AI talent” if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills. There may be a will to also count “implied skills”, i.e. for people in occupations that assume AI expertise even if they haven’t tagged it on their profile, but by and large the lens remains mainly technical. Women’s share of C-suite roles held by AI talent at AI companies is stated to be 13%. But it leaves out government and civil society as well as leaders within the AI industry who don’t hold technical titles.

In a recent development, skills raise the same question. LinkedIn separates AI literacy, meaning the use of tools like ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot, from the engineering skills needed to build the technology. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she didn’t know whether it is counted at all, “because it’s not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool that you would be using.”.

Sources indicate that we have seen this before. The previous generation of tech jobs was measured with coding as the yardstick, and women who ran product, policy, or trust and safety teams barely indicated up in the count.

According to recent reports, if leadership means making decisions that change the course of AI, many of those decisions are now made outside AI companies. On Nov. 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all of which aimed at limiting construction. Voters approved nearly all of them.

And women are prominent in these fights. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George’s County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum’s petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project. In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June.

The revolt is likely to change the industry. It is “forcing a lot of AI leaders to have to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public,” Steinberg said. When companies arrive in towns and ask local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements, on the assumption that residents would welcome a transformative technology, “what they’re finding is that the benefits that people are experiencing from this technology are not outweighing the negatives that having a data center in their community would present,” she added. Data centers do create some jobs, she added, but “whether that is at a level that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide.”.

Europe tells a similar story. Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU’s work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office. In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50 % of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules.

It’s true that some of the best-known critics of the industry, like Timnit Gebru, did not choose to stand outside the AI industry: they were pushed out. Women end up regulating and contesting AI because public-sector, legal, and community careers are more inclusive, while the best-paid technical jobs remain largely in the hands of tech bros who perpetuate a culture that actively filters women out.

It has been revealed that another blind spot is usage: women may use AI more than they admit. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code. When told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price: a 13% drop in perceived competence, compared with 6% for men. Because of this “hidden penalty of using AI”, any measure of AI skills based on self-reporting is likely to miss all the women who choose not to mention their use and their skills.

Sources indicate that steinberg also pointed to the skills employers now want. Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation, conflict management. She is bullish on women’s strengths there, but she warned that “we haven’t really figured out the code” to train, evaluate, and promote people on those skills. Until we do, that contribution will remain mostly invisible too.

Recent findings suggest that none of this is an argument for complacency. Women should be building AI tools and running AI companies, where decisions about capital and products are made. A 13% share of C-suite AI leadership roles is a disaster. And LinkedIn’s data can help better fight this fight. Because it tracks how people move from job to job, it shows where women drop off, and the answer varies by industry. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite. Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level. In STEM, it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job.

Sources indicate that but a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation, and everyday use. If we could map the gap across industry, government, and civil society, we would have a better baseline, and it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest.

Neuralink trial participant ditches mouth stick to play GTA 6 with his mind

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk’s Neuralink started clinical trials less than three years ago, and patients are seeing impressive results.
  • Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink https://t.co/ViFjXK9OSVNovember 20, 2026.
  • It has been revealed that the first Neuralink device was implanted in January 2024, with the patient able to move a mouse just by thinking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk’s Neuralink started clinical trials less than three years ago, and patients are seeing impressive results. The latest demonstration of this brain computer interface comes via a video on social media showing an unnamed medical trial participant playing GTA 6. According to the video, the team behind the implant mapped different i,agined movements to a PlayStation 5 controller, allowing the player to simulate controller actions using his thoughts. For example, thinking about tapping their ring finger activated the square button while imagining sliding their right hand forward pulled the nose of the airplane up. They also mentioned another control being bound to their foot, it’s unclear what action this allowed.

Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink https://t.co/ViFjXK9OSVNovember 20, 2026.

It has been revealed that the first Neuralink device was implanted in January 2024, with the patient able to move a mouse just by thinking. Once they’ve been able to master the basics of using a computer, like moving a mouse and using the keyboard, through the brain-computer interface (BCI), one of the next steps that some patients take is to play a game on their system. Just a couple of months after the first implant, we’ve already seen reports of people using Neuralink to play turn-based games like chess and Civilization VI. By August 2024, the second Neuralink recipient was reportedly playing Counter-Strike 2, with the patient calling the experience “insane.”.

Today, we already have people playing complicated games like World of Warcraft and GTA VI using BCI implants. This is an achievement for Neuralink and a life-changing capability for patients who have lost mobility. The patient who streamed their GTA VI gameplay said that they’ve previously used a mouth stick, but it was miles away from the Neuralink chip they have in their head. “Before the … chip and surgery, I was using a mouth stick and an iPad. I was essentially like a bird just pecking at an iPad. There was (sic) like a few games I could play, but like obviously it made your jaw sore, it made everything sore,” the patient said. “So, then I get a chip, and I was like what does this let me do. Immediately, controlling a computer is like boom, ‘portal to the world,’ like you just immediately get your portal to the world back.”.

It has been revealed that aside from giving people the ability to control computing devices with their mind, Neuralink is also working on a technology, called Blindsight, that will restore sight to blind people. Musk claims that it’s already “ready from an engineering standpoint,” and that the tech giant is only waiting for regulatory approval before it can begin human testing.

#104451. How to keep AI from turning your organization into the Borg

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3214 w)
