How to keep AI from turning your organization into the Borg

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a big fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
  • In a recent development, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a substantial fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
  • In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a big fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation. While I enjoyed the stories, what really stuck with me in an enduring way was the ethos of the show, and especially what it had to say about how to lead when long-term principles and immediate goals pull in different directions. The death last month of Sir Patrick Stewart—the actor behind the inimitable Captain Picard—sent me back to watch some old episodes of the show. It is perhaps unsurprising that the episodes that stood out to me were those in which the captain and his crew confronted the Borg, a collective of formerly independent life forms who had become fused together into a single hive mind. In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology. The hive’s drones carried the knowledge of every civilization the collective had absorbed but lacked anything in the way of individuality: they had no name, no will, and no ideas of their own. The first time I watched the episodes, I saw them as a thought-provoking and dystopian fantasy. Today, they strike me as delivering an essential warning about the dangers of AI. The Borg chased perfection through uniformity. AI seems to be sending humans along a similar, worrying trajectory. The homogenizing effect of AI Language models are trained to predict the most likely next word in a sequence, then tuned to give the kinds of answers people rate highly. The result is output that is fluent, competent, and increasingly alike. And when millions of people and thousands of companies lean on the same few models, that sameness spreads. In a 2025 study named after the Borg’s defining image of a hivemind, researchers tested more than 70 language models on real-world, open-ended questions. They found striking similarities both within models and between models—individual models repeated themselves, while groups of models collectively converged on the same responses. For example, when 25 models (from the US, China, and elsewhere) were asked 50 times to provide a metaphor about time, most of the responses were variants of time being either a river or a weaver. By contrast, when a reporter at the MIT Technology Review asked six of their (human) colleagues the same thing, they got six different answers with nary a mention of rivers or weavers. This commonality reaches beyond the texts that LLMs output themselves. In September this year, Nature rounded up a fast-growing body of research suggesting that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write, and possibly how we think. In one study it cited, students who used ChatGPT on creative tasks for just five days were still giving more similar answers months later, even when they didn’t use AI. Business is showing early signs of the same phenomenon. A recent study of earnings-call transcripts found that companies’ prepared remarks have grown strikingly similar as AI writing tools have spread, and that more uniform language was associated with more negative initial market reactions. The irony is striking. Each company is betting that AI will make it sharper. But collectively AI seems to be making business duller and more standardized. The leaders who win in this new world will be those who find ways to capture the benefits AI can offer to individuals without falling into the trap of becoming part of the collective. Picard’s encounters with the Borg offer three lessons in how to do that. Don’t become a mouthpiece In “The Best of Both Worlds,” the Borg capture Picard and turn him into a drone they call Locutus, their spokesman. Picard’s face and voice announce decisions that are no longer his, but that come instead from the collective hivemind. Leaders may already be drifting in this direction. In IBM’s 2026 CEO study of 2,000 CEOs, 64% mentioned they are “comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI-generated input.” Further, they expect AI to make 48% of operational decisions without human intervention by 2030, up from 25% today. Unchecked delegation to AI can end up being very expensive. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the roughly $290,000 it was paid for a government report that contained apparent AI-generated errors such as imaginary research and made-up quotes from federal courts. More insiduously, the skills that let leaders catch such errors can fade promptly. In a randomized trial published by Anthropic in January, developers who learned a new programming tool with AI assistance scored 17% lower on a quiz about the tool than those who had acquired their knowledge by themselves. Deloitte itself is a case in point. Last month, a year after that first refund, the government of Western Australia demanded an expedited refund from Deloitte for a study on merging three of the state’s universities. The firm had disclosed using generative AI to help gather research, summarize information, and proofread content, but the report nevertheless turned out to contain errors such as a simple miscalculation that reduced cost estimates by 260 million AUD, references to sources that did not exist, and using a name for one of the universities that had been “changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.” The takeaway: Delegate the analysis, keep the judgment. Anyone who signs off on an AI recommendation should be able to explain why it is right—and this should extend to personal ownership of all the constituent details. Protect the people who disagree The Borg instantiated the promise of a certain type of harmony: no drone ever argued with the collective for the simple reason that there was nothing to argue about. All drones thought the same thoughts and held exactly the same beliefs. This made the Borg both formidably efficient and dangerously blind. AI can build a version of that consensus into an organization. A recent Stanford-led study found that 11 leading AI systems affirmed users’ actions 49% more frequently than did other humans, even when those actions involved deception or harm. A single affirming response made people more convinced they were right and less willing to take responsibility for their decision. Worse, participants rated flattering and non-flattering responses as about equally objective. “The very feature that causes harm also drives engagement,” the authors wrote. An organization in which every manager has a tireless assistant telling them they’re right is an organization slowly losing its capacity to disagree. On the show, the Borg’s uniformity is eventually broken by a single drone. Rescued by Picard’s crew, a drone they name Hugh develops a sense of self, and after he is sent home, this threat to the collective spreads to other drones.Yet left without support, the newly independent drones quickly fall under the control of a manipulative new leader. Independent thinking is both contagious and fragile. The takeaway: If your AI tends to agree with you, you will need to turn to other people for disagreement. Treat dissent as infrastructure. Reward the person who pushes back, and back them when they are right. Individuality without support is easily undermined. Rebuilding takes more than retraining The crew rescues Picard from the Borg quickly but it takes him much longer to become himself again. After being rescued, he goes home to his family’s vineyard in France, unsure who he is and tempted to quit Starfleet. No debriefing or new assignment puts him back together. His brother does, in a quarrel that ends with Picard finally breaking down. It takes time, and it takes family. When companies blueprint for what AI will do to their people, they tend to plan for skills: who needs retraining, and on which tools. Far less attention goes to the meaning and purpose that people find in work. A study published in March found that people who relied passively on AI to do their work found less meaning in it, and that the loss appeared to carry over into the work they later did on their own. And in an October survey by Elon University, 70% of U.S. workers said paid work is extremely or very crucial to their sense of meaning and purpose, and 65% of Americans agreed that if AI makes work less meaningful, people will lose their sense of purpose and dignity. As with Picard, much of the rebuilding happens through people. In the same survey, workers said that if AI substantially affects their jobs, they would place more faith in the people close to them than in formal organizations. Yet AI is quietly thinning those relationships at work. A recent piece in Harvard Business Review that surveyed just over 1,000 U.S. workers reported that AI was reducing communication within teams and thereby significantly reducing team trust and coordination. So the bonds are fraying just as people need them more than ever before. The takeaway: Budget for rebuilding purpose alongside retraining. Give people time to adjust, and protect the relationships they will lean on while they do. Track whether people still find meaning in their work as carefully as you track whether they can use the tools. Resistance is the point The Borg’s catchphrase was “Resistance is futile.” Patrick Stewart’s Picard proved them wrong, mostly by being stubbornly, unmistakably himself. And in that lies a crucial lesson for business leaders. AI is a remarkably useful tool. But it nudges everyone who uses it toward the same safe answer, and a company that stops noticing will end up thinking, sounding, and deciding like everyone else. Pushing back against that pull is now part of a leader’s job. Nobody else is going to do it.

#104450. ‘Sex sells, fellas’: President Trump defends Jensen Huang, says he pushed for him to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO

‘Sex sells, fellas’: President Trump defends Jensen Huang, says he pushed for him to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate manufacturer president and CEO Jensen Huang.
  • President Donald Trump indicates he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate tech giant president and CEO Jensen Huang.
  • On Monday morning, Nvidia confirmed that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate manufacturer president and CEO Jensen Huang. On Monday morning, Nvidia declared that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation. “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement on the latest development. The decision comes as multiple investigations—including those from the Justice Department and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission—are still ongoing. And just last week, Nvidia chairman Harvey ​Jones had said that the company would not rehire Huang, given that his conduct did not meet the company’s code of conduct. Huang had stepped down as CEO after allegedly having an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as an additional affair with a subordinate. But after Monday’s stunning decision to reinstate Huang, Trump seemingly took some credit for the move, telling the media that he advocated for the briefly jobless boss to come back into power. Trump told CNBC that Huang “did nothing wrong,” and said that he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” ahead of the move, making clear that he argued on behalf of the CEO. The product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

It has been revealed that then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:.

Sources indicate that build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:.

In a recent development, with some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot indicates the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

In a recent development, the real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the newly introduced product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

Those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern.

I’d revise the original prompt like this:.

Sources indicate that build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the latest product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

According to recent reports, the extra detail also gives you a review proposal. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:.

In a recent development, AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

Each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

The next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

#104444. Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2848 w)
📖 Baca

Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
  • According to recent reports, the Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
  • Sources indicate that strogatz is no ordinary mathematician.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay, the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better? Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime Latest York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem. The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written). Clearly, today we are living in our own version of the infinite monkey theorem, which is what Strogatz was getting at in his Atlantic piece. If you can have infinite agents attacking every aspect of an age-old problem, solving it over a period of hours, what is the value of a mathematician’s work? Is it even worth pursuing? Borges, in his story The Library of Babel, gave us—and mathematicians like Strogatz—some guidance about creating value in a world of infinite monkeys. First, there is the problem of curation. Yes, infinite monkeys could write War and Peace, but good luck finding it amongst all the flotsam and jetsam. We’re seeing the problem in real life today. While AI should theoretically be ramping up productivity, in reality, workers are drowning in workslop. The second problem is that of intent. War and Peace isn’t just meaningful for the words it contains, but because of what Leo Tolstoy intended when he wrote them. In much the same way, while it is true that artificial intelligence can run circles around human mathematicians, it is also true that humans chose the problems that OpenAI solved, and they chose them because humans found them meaningful and, possibly, useful. So one way that mathematicians—or anyone else—can find meaning and value in the age of AI is by acting as curators and as principal agents. Humans can choose the work that gets done according to what is meaningful to them and other humans. You could see the seeds of that idea in Strogatz’s piece. Even if all problems are solvable, we still need to choose which ones we want to solve. Principle 2: The economics of automation Another way to think about how you find meaning and create value in the age of AI is to analyze the economics of automation. One effective framework involves examining three constituent forces: the displacement effect, the productivity effect, and the reinstatement effect. Together, they can help us determine where threats and opportunities might lie. The displacement effect refers to jobs that are replaced by an automating technology—in this case, AI. The productivity effect refers to the increase in output per given unit of input due to the technological advance. The reinstatement effect refers to new jobs made possible by a technological advance. To understand how the three effects work together, it’s helpful to look at the life of Henry Ford. Growing up on a family farm, young Henry would once have been expected to remain in the fields. But as agricultural productivity increased, he had more opportunities beyond the farm. He eventually went to work for Thomas Edison and later created an entirely new automobile industry, reinstating millions of jobs both directly and indirectly. In the case of Henry Ford, the story was a happy one. The productivity and reinstatement effects dwarfed the displacement effect and everybody, for the most part, was better off. But the AI data is fuzzy. We are certainly seeing early signs of the displacement effect as people lose jobs, but so far we’ve seen few signs of a significant productivity or reinstatement effect. Still, understanding the economics of automation can help us find value and meaning. Clearly, with answers to tough problems so much more accessible, mathematicians—and other experts—can help the rest of us formulate good problems to apply to real-world challenges. Some value will likely shift from solving problems to finding good questions. 3. Jevons Paradox and the O-Ring model During the Industrial Revolution—which the AI age is often compared to—James Watt’s steam engine used coal much more efficiently than Thomas Newcomen’s version. So, many assumed that coal use would go down. But English economist William Stanley Jevons saw that just the opposite was happening. Coal use was actually increasing. Ever since, that phenomenon has been known as the Jevons paradox, the effect that occurs when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource’s use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in its use. If price elasticity is high enough, the decrease in costs encourages people to find more uses for that resource and demand increases. Another useful concept is the O-ring theory of economic development, which gets its name from the Challenger space shuttle disaster. The shuttle, for the most part, was in good working order, but a malfunction in an O-ring seal due to unusually cold weather led to a massive midair explosion. The point is that every job is made up of many interdependent tasks, and if even a single one fails, the entire thing doesn’t work. We’re seeing signs of both effects in the AI economy. While software developers can outsource many coding tasks to AI, they still need humans for others, such as communicating and collaborating with other experts on the team. Nevertheless, with code being produced so much more efficiently, job postings for software developers are on the rise. Strogatz may find something similar happening in mathematics. After all, there are many facets of his job that don’t involve developing proofs. He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve important problems with mathematical insights. The future of technology is always more human Technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained. Yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off. Today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a new age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as important as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly. The good news is that we have good tools to help us navigate our way through. The infinite monkey theorem highlights the importance of curation and intent. The economics of automation reveals the need for productivity growth to finance reinstatement. The Jevons paradox and the O-ring model encourage us to identify our place within increasingly complex ecosystems. AI can give us answers, but it can’t tell us what questions we want to ask. In the future, that’s where human value and meaning will increasingly lie.

According to recent reports, the Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay, the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better?

Sources indicate that strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime Upcoming York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out.

Recent findings suggest that the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem. The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written).

Clearly, today we are living in our own version of the infinite monkey theorem, which is what Strogatz was getting at in his Atlantic piece. If you can have infinite agents attacking every aspect of an age-old problem, solving it over a period of hours, what is the value of a mathematician’s work? Is it even worth pursuing?

Industry observers note that borges, in his story The Library of Babel, gave us—and mathematicians like Strogatz—some guidance about creating value in a world of infinite monkeys. First, there is the problem of curation. Yes, infinite monkeys could write War and Peace, but good luck finding it amongst all the flotsam and jetsam. We’re seeing the problem in real life today. While AI should theoretically be ramping up productivity, in reality, workers are drowning in workslop.

The second problem is that of intent. War and Peace isn’t just meaningful for the words it contains, but because of what Leo Tolstoy intended when he wrote them. In much the same way, while it is true that artificial intelligence can run circles around human mathematicians, it is also true that humans chose the problems that OpenAI solved, and they chose them because humans found them meaningful and, possibly, useful.

In a recent development, so one way that mathematicians—or anyone else—can find meaning and value in the age of AI is by acting as curators and as principal agents. Humans can choose the work that gets done according to what is meaningful to them and other humans. You could see the seeds of that idea in Strogatz’s piece. Even if all problems are solvable, we still need to choose which ones we want to solve.

Another way to think about how you find meaning and create value in the age of AI is to analyze the economics of automation. One effective framework involves examining three constituent forces: the displacement effect, the productivity effect, and the reinstatement effect. Together, they can help us determine where threats and opportunities might lie.

According to recent reports, the displacement effect refers to jobs that are replaced by an automating technology—in this case, AI. The productivity effect refers to the increase in output per given unit of input due to the technological advance. The reinstatement effect refers to upcoming jobs made possible by a technological advance.

Recent findings suggest that to understand how the three effects work together, it’s helpful to look at the life of Henry Ford. Growing up on a family farm, young Henry would once have been expected to remain in the fields. But as agricultural productivity increased, he had more opportunities beyond the farm. He eventually went to work for Thomas Edison and later created an entirely newly introduced automobile industry, reinstating millions of jobs both directly and indirectly.

In the case of Henry Ford, the story was a happy one. The productivity and reinstatement effects dwarfed the displacement effect and everybody, for the most part, was better off. But the AI data is fuzzy. We are certainly seeing early signs of the displacement effect as people lose jobs, but so far we’ve seen few signs of a significant productivity or reinstatement effect.

Still, understanding the economics of automation can help us find value and meaning. Clearly, with answers to tough problems so much more accessible, mathematicians—and other experts—can help the rest of us formulate good problems to apply to real-world challenges. Some value will likely shift from solving problems to finding good questions.

It has been revealed that during the Industrial Revolution—which the AI age is often compared to—James Watt’s steam engine used coal much more efficiently than Thomas Newcomen’s version. So, many assumed that coal use would go down. But English economist William Stanley Jevons saw that just the opposite was happening. Coal use was actually increasing.

Recent findings suggest that ever since, that phenomenon has been known as the Jevons paradox, the effect that occurs when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource’s use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in its use. If price elasticity is high enough, the decrease in costs encourages people to find more uses for that resource and demand increases.

According to recent reports, another useful concept is the O-ring theory of economic development, which gets its name from the Challenger space shuttle disaster. The shuttle, for the most part, was in good working order, but a malfunction in an O-ring seal due to unusually cold weather led to a massive midair explosion. The point is that every job is made up of many interdependent tasks, and if even a single one fails, the entire thing doesn’t work.

Sources indicate that we’re seeing signs of both effects in the AI economy. While software developers can outsource many coding tasks to AI, they still need humans for others, such as communicating and collaborating with other experts on the team. Nevertheless, with code being produced so much more efficiently, job postings for software developers are on the rise.

Strogatz may find something similar happening in mathematics. After all, there are many facets of his job that don’t involve developing proofs. He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve important problems with mathematical insights.

It has been revealed that technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained.

It has been revealed that yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off.

According to recent reports, today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a new age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as crucial as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly.

Lenovo Pro 9n review: 18-core RTX Spark in a fancy chassis

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lenovo Pro 9n is an elegant consumer workstation with a vivid OLED screen and lots of ports, but it's expensive, and RTX Spark still needs to differentiate itself with Windows features to justify that price.
  • Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Industry observers note that A lot of noise was made about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, but there's a handful of other premium machines running Nvidia's newly introduced RTX Spark chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lenovo Pro 9n is an elegant consumer workstation with a vivid OLED screen and lots of ports, but it's expensive, and RTX Spark still needs to differentiate itself with Windows features to justify that price.

Lighter than Surface Laptop Ultra.

ExpensiveBattery life could be better.

Included stylus doesn't work on the touchscreen.

Windows doesn't take advantage of RTX Spark.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Industry observers note that A lot of noise was made about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, but there's a handful of other premium machines running Nvidia's newly introduced RTX Spark chips. Lenovo's Pro 9n follows Microsoft's lead, making a fancy laptop with its own touches, like an OLED panel and a stylus that works on the touchpad.

This is also our first time looking at the 18-core version of the RTX Spark, which has fewer CUDA cores than the last one we tested, so we'll see just what kind of changes in performance you get if you don't opt for a higher-end configuration.

The Lenovo Pro 9n is clearly a tool. It's a dark gray box with a Lenovo logo and a slight extrusion to fit Lenovo's signature anti-notch for the camera. The lid is flat, with a rounded keyboard deck, like many of Lenovo's premium Yoga laptops. It's a playful look that's less noticeable when the system is matte black rather than colorful.

The keyboard deck, including a massive touchpad, is logo-free other than an Nvidia RTX Spark sticker, which keeps all of your attention on the backlit keyboard and 15.3-inch OLED screen.

There are plenty of ports, and I appreciate that both sides of the laptop have both USB Type-C and Type-A. The left side also has HDMI and a 3.5 mm headphone jack, while the right side includes an SD card slot and an e-shutter for the webcam.

At 13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches, this isn't a small system, but it's still one you can reasonably fit in your backpack. It's wider and deeper than the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra (12.95 x 9.40 x 0.75 inches) but it's also thinner. Apple's new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is a tad sleeker at 0.63 inches thick.

It has been revealed that the Pro 9n measured in at 3.64 pounds pounds, less than 4.41-pound Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra. The 16-inch MacBook Pro is a bit heavier than the Pro 9n at 4.1 pounds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

5,120 CUDA cores, Blackwell-based.

15.3-inch, 2560 x 1600, OLED, touch, 165 Hz.

MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 MT7925, Bluetooth 5.4.

HDMI 2.1, 2s USB Type-A (10Gbps), 2x USB4 Type-C (40 Gbps), 3.5 mm headphone jack, SD card reader (UHS-II).

13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches / 347 mm x 242 mm x 16.7 mm.

The Lenovo Pro 9n features the lesser variant of the RTX Spark N1X, and this is our first look at a system with that config. This version has an 18-core CPU, down from the 20-core version we saw with the Surface Laptop Ultra. It also has 32GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.

On Geekbench 6, the Pro 9n came in slightly behind the Surface Laptop in both single-core and multi-core performance (given how heavy the Surface Laptop is, some of this could come down to cooling). The MacBook Pro with M5 Max won out, while the Asus ZenBook A16 with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme beat both RTX Sparks.

Recent findings suggest that the Pro 9n copied 25GB of files at a rate of 1,205.37 MBps. That's not terrible, but in the ultra-premium price band, you can get faster speeds. Every other laptop beat the Pro 9n here.

Recent findings suggest that on Handbrake, the Pro 9n transcoded a 4K video to 1080p in 2 minutes and 1 second, or 7 seconds behind the Surface Pro with the 20-core CPU. The Pro 9n beat the Snapdragon-powered Zenbook here.

We use Cinebench 2026 to stress test laptops, running a multi-core benchmark ten times in a row. The Pro 9n stayed largely consistent — in fact, it even got better later on, as the cooling kicked into high gear. The system started with a score of 6,219.85, and topped out on run 6 at 6,417.45. Most of the runs were in the high 6,300s. The RTX Spark's Cortex-A725 cores ran at an average of 2.81 GHz, while the Cortex-X925 cores averaged 3.57 GHz.

It's worth noting that HWinfo, which we used for monitoring, was missing a single A725 core. This also happened on the Surface Laptop Ultra, though now we can tell which cores are which.

The Lenovo Pro 9n we reviewed came with the entry-level version of Nvidia's RTX Spark, which has an 18-core CPU and 5,120 CUDA cores. It can be upgraded to a 20-core / 6,144 CUDA core chip in some configurations, which is the same chip we saw in the Surface Laptop Ultra.

To test the difference in AI performance, we ran AgentPerf-Local using Qwen 3.8-27B-UD_IQ3_XXS in order to fit in the limited available GPU memory (both are 32GB systems, with the Surface allowing 24GB of allocated graphics memory and the Pro 9n accepting just 16GB). The benchmark simulates running conversations by playing back conversations, with a majority of the work involving processing prompts rather than generating tokens.

In a recent development, the difference between the two RTX Spark systems wasn't particularly significant here. The Surface Laptop Ultra completed the benchmark in 1,148.3 seconds, while the Pro 9n took 1,196.6 seconds. That's a 4.12% difference in favor of the higher-end Spark.

It has been revealed that beyond the difference in CPU cores, the version of RTX Spark in the Pro 9n we tested has 5,120 CUDA cores, down from 6,144 in the more powerful version in the Surface Laptop Ultra. (The beefier chip is also available in other configurations of the Pro 9n).

On 3DMark Steel Nomad, the Pro 9n earned a score of 2,796, falling behind the Laptop Ultra (4,355) and the MacBook Pro (3,865). It's still a more powerful system than the Zenbook with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme (1,262).

Recent findings suggest that in gaming, the RTX Spark isn't really meant for much above 1080p (perhaps 1440p, depending on the game). So in the case of our benchmarks, the difference in CUDA cores didn't have a stark difference, with nearly identical scores on Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077. Far Cry 6, which is more CPU-focused, ran better on the 20-core RTX Spark.

When I played 007: First Light, with the game at 1920 x 1200 and settings on medium, and DLSS set to ultra performance, the game ran just over 30 frames per second. With DLSS on "dynamic," the game ran smoother, between 40 and 72 frames per second as Bond moved through a swanky hotel, though there was some jankiness to it. The game also took a long time to load, possibly due to Windows' Prism emulation.

In a recent development, the 15.3-inch OLED touchscreen on the Pro 9n is quite nice. The 165 Hz panel is vivid and bright enough for most uses.

The trailer for Artificial demonstrated off the colors and blacks, as the trailer descends from lush greens outside of Sam Altman's home to a dark tunnel, until he arrives in a bunker with blue lights that all but jumped off the screen.

According to recent reports, lenovo's OLED panel was the most vivid of our test group on our colorimeter, covering 198% of the sRGB color space by volume, significantly higher than the rest of the field, though it often appeared oversaturated. In fact, it arrivees out of the box on its default wallpaper with severe pops of green and white. The MacBook Pro's PROLED XDR display has lower numbers on the colorimeter, but looks far more natural than what Lenovo is offering here.

At 440.6 nits of brightness, the Pro 9n's display is good, but the MacBook Pro has it beat at 529.5 nits, while the Surface Laptop Pro reached an astounding 944 nits in our testing.

Lenovo's keyboard feels great. There's 1.5 mm of key travel, and you can feel it. It's deep, but punchy. The keycaps can be a bit slippery, though I typed at 106 words per minute on the monkeytype typing test, albeit with 2% less accuracy than usual.

The haptic touchpad is huge, smooth, and responsive. Oddly enough, despite being haptic, there is a noticeable depression when you click down, especially at the bottom edge. It's an odd feeling when you notice it, especially when you can still configure how hard you have to press in Windows to register a click.

Industry observers note that lenovo includes a stylus in the box for use with the touch screen, which is good for signing documents. The pen, however, does not work on the touchscreen, which is an odd choice. The Yoga Pen Gen 2 (typically sold for $63 with a case that isn't included here) can attach magnetically to the Pro 9n's lid and charges over USB Type-C, so you can use the same charger as the laptop. It supports up to 8,192 points of pressure sensitivity with AES3.0, or up to 4,096 points on other protocols.

Lenovo's combination of two tweeters and two woofers does a decent job. They get nice and loud, easily filling a mid-sized office room with Justice's "Flower In A Hurricane.".

The song's guitars and synths sounded excellent, as did SZA and Kevin Parker's voices. The drum beat was a bit low, but going into the Dolby Settings app, switching to the "Warm" music setting with boosted lows helped there.

There are 9 screws holding the bottom of the Lenovo Pro 9n on. The four closest to the hinge are longer than the remaining five, so be sure to keep them organized. You'll need a pry tool to remove the latches and release the base.

Sources indicate that inside, there's not a ton to repair or replace down the line for the average person. The 92.5 WHr battery is held in place with a few screws. You can also easily access the included M.2 2242 SSD, and there's a second bay for another drive of the same length. I would always prefer a more standard 2280 drive, but if this is what lets Lenovo fit two drives on the board (or at least give you the option to add a second drive), I'll take it.

The Wi-Fi card is soldered to the board and partially obscured by the heatsink's thick heat pipes.

The Pro 9n ran for 10 hours and 30 minutes on average on our battery test, which browses the web, streams video from a server, and runs OpenGL tests with the screen set to 150 nits of brightness.

That's not too far off from other high-end Windows on Arm laptops, beating the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme-based Zenbook A16 by 4 minutes, and it was 13 minutes behind the Surface Laptop Ultra with a more powerful version of N1X.

The MacBook Pro smoked them all though, running for 15 hours and 57 minutes on our test.

During our Cinebench stress test, we took skin temperature measurements to get an idea of how hot the Pro 9n gets during use.

The center of the keyboard measured 98.5 degrees Fahrenheit, while the touchpad was 10 degrees cooler. The hottest point on the bottom of the laptop reached 101.5 F.

In a recent development, HWinfo hasn't been updated to be clear on which sensors are measuring what internally. We could make educated guesses, but we'll have more specifics when the software is updated.

The 9.2-megapixel webcam on the Pro 9n should be more than enough for video calling in 4K, assuming your software supports it. While making calls, I found that the camera captured fine details, like graying hairs on the side of my temples (it's been a long month).

The colors were a bit cool, however. I could do with more vibrancy and warmth to make it more realistic.

Industry observers note that there’s just too much pre-loaded software on the Pro 9n. The most notable app is Vantage, a catch-all app with your serial number, user guides, warranty status, a number of device settings, and access to support services. But it also houses a ton of ads.

Recent findings suggest that the company also has direct links in the Start menu and taskbar to the Lenovo subscription portal to buy software. An additional user guide is also in the start menu. There's also Smart Connect, to pair and transfer files between your laptop, tablet, and phone, along with a dashboard to view them all. The company also has its stylus settings app and a link in the Start Menu to its Artificial Intelligence policy, which looks more like an internal document than something meant for consumers.

Lenovo also includes some bloatware, like trials of McAfee antivirus and a promotional trial of Dropbox.

Like other RTX Spark systems, the Pro 9n is running Windows on Arm. It's better than it's ever been, but there are still times when it feels laggy. More games and apps than before are compatible, but it's still not perfect.

Lenovo sells the Pro 9n with a 1-year warranty, which can be extended with additional coverage for more money.

We tested the Lenovo Pro 9n in a $3,249.99 configuration with an 18-core RTX Spark CPU and integrated GPU using 5,120 CUDA cores, 32GB of RAM, a 1TB PCIe Gen 4 SSD, and Windows 11 Pro.

The cheapest version, at $2,999.99, uses the same processor and RAM as our review unit, comes with Windows 11 Home, and has 512GB of RAM.

It has been revealed that bumping up to the higher-end 20-core, 6,144 CUDA-core GPU costs an extra $450 but also gets you 64GB of RAM and 1TB of storage as a base. Moving to 128GB of RAM is $1,400, while moving to a 2TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD is another $450.

The Lenovo Pro 9n is a minimalist, RTX Spark-based laptop with strong port selection and a lovely OLED screen. The keyboard has deep travel, and I don't mind a design that simply gets out of the way of your work.

According to recent reports, still, it's expensive, even with the base version of RTX Spark. Battery life is just past 10 hours, which I would like to see improve across the RTX Spark platform, and there aren't any AI features in Windows that make this chip special for anyone who isn't running local models.

Recent findings suggest that if you are married to getting an RTX Spark machine, the Lenovo Pro 9n beats the Surface Laptop Ultra in three areas: It's lighter, has an OLED screen, and extra SSD slots (even if it is M.2 2242) for an upgrade down the line. Still, the Surface is a nicer, more premium design and has the fun, magnetic Surface Connect port.

Those who aren't running local models should probably be looking for a cheaper laptop. Those prioritizing battery life should consider a Mac. And those who like Windows on Arm can still consider Snapdragon X2, as Nvidia's entrance into this choppy sea should lift all ships.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.
  • Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.
  • No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares. No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year. On top of all that, there’s concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Flight delays and cancellations The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by fresh system failures. First there was the Federal Aviation Administration’s network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays. Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said. As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed. Round-trip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper. Wicked weather on both coasts Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s midsection, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center. Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day, and reach Maine by Friday, he said. The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph). The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an problem. “This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.” Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides. Thanksgiving snow for some in the U.S. Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning, with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said. Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state, and northwestern Pennsylvania. “Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.” —By John Seewer, Associated Press Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack and Dave Collins contributed to this story.

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.

No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.

On top of all that, there’s concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

It has been revealed that first there was the Federal Aviation Administration’s network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.

Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.

“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline mentioned.

As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware noted 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.

Round-trip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking organization Hopper.

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s midsection, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

It has been revealed that many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the Fresh York City area on Thanksgiving Day, and reach Maine by Friday, he mentioned.

Industry observers note that the windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).

The weather service said it expected the rain in Fresh York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.

In a recent development, “This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”.

Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning, with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.

Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western Newly introduced York state, and northwestern Pennsylvania.

Recent findings suggest that “Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”.

—By John Seewer, Associated Press.

Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack and Dave Collins contributed to this story.

#104439. Industry News: How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3960 w)

Industry News: How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a upcoming app on their phone and keep it open during their shift.
  • It has been revealed that corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a latest app on their phone and keep it open during their shift.
  • The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a upcoming app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see. The app uses technology from Drivosity, a firm that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering, and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney mentioned.As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.”  Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer, and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime’s ability to track workers in real time, down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores. Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment. Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior—how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom—into data that can score, rank, discipline, and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers, and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring. “They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools. * * * In February, Burger King revealed that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with intends to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders. “It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez. Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly. Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added. Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini” [Google’s AI assistant].“The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.” Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations time-stamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores. Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.”  According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities. Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity, or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias. The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year. Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it. He quit in August. “If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.” * * * While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies—Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC, and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts”—a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility. Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys, and other chains. Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock, or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts. In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law. Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.” * * * While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores, and ranks all employees. Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests,” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange, they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions.When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores. Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored, and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.” MashMore at the moment has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.” * * * Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on September 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff. Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty—but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.”  Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.”Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off. When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing. Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.” —By Z Waite This piece was originally published by Capital & Main.

#104437. Abdul El-Sayed rebranded ‘Medicare for All’ to get Trump’s attention. It worked

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1164 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Abdul El-Sayed rebranded ‘Medicare for All’ to get Trump’s attention. It worked

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan campaigned on passing “Medicare for All,” a universal single-payer national health insurance system.
  • Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan campaigned on passing “Medicare for All,” a universal single-payer national health insurance system.
  • In mid-November, El Sayed posted an image on social media of a gold card emblazoned with the name “TrumpCare.” The mock-up was a convincing depiction of what a TrumpCare insurance card might look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan campaigned on passing “Medicare for All,” a universal single-payer national health insurance system. He believes in the initiative so much that he’s even willing to rebrand it to an unlikely name. In mid-November, El Sayed posted an image on social media of a gold card emblazoned with the name “TrumpCare.” The mock-up was a convincing depiction of what a TrumpCare insurance card might look like. Trump’s name and signature are in the bottom right-hand corner, and there’s a presidential-style seal as well as the tagline “Great Health Care for Every American.” “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote on X on November 12. The card was designed to get President Donald Trump’s attention—and it did. On Saturday, Trump reshared a screenshot of the card on his social network, Truth Social, without adding a comment of his own. Vice President JD Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting, NBC News reported Sunday. This is a message for @realDonaldTrump. Donald, this is on the table. Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan campaigned on passing “Medicare for All,” a universal single-payer national health insurance system. He believes in the initiative so much that he’s even willing to rebrand it to an unlikely name.

In mid-November, El Sayed posted an image on social media of a gold card emblazoned with the name “TrumpCare.” The mock-up was a convincing depiction of what a TrumpCare insurance card might look like. Trump’s name and signature are in the bottom right-hand corner, and there’s a presidential-style seal as well as the tagline “Great Health Care for Every American.”.

“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote on X on November 12.

It has been revealed that the card was designed to get President Donald Trump’s attention—and it did. On Saturday, Trump reshared a screenshot of the card on his social network, Truth Social, without adding a comment of his own. Vice President JD Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting, NBC News reported Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A wall of 100 Noctua PC fans was built by maker Sasa Karanovic because "why not." There's a little more to it, though, as the Toronto-based electronics and 3D printing expert wanted to test the capabilities of his new open-source open-hardware OpenFAN XL fan controller. A video highlights the setup and control of a 10x10 Noctua fan grid controlled via the 10 headers on the controller. A 50x2 setup was also shown working off the controller. Karanovic indicates that 100 fans was "no sweat" for the new controller, but it would max out at around 200 spinners in its current iteration.

In a recent development, the maker explains in the video that they had this demo idea a while back but recently acquired 100 fans through a combination of "a ton of luck and a good friend." As the latest OpenFAN XL controller has 10 headers, the natural first step in controlling them all was to make a grid of 10 x 10 units. That's a lot of fans, but there's also 200 fan grills, 800 screws, and oodles of wiring, including tens of fan splitters.

So, the 100 fans aren't individually controllable, they are controlled in banks of 10 due to the 10 header channels. Thus, the granularity of control on offer here can only apply to 10 fans at the fewest in an array of 100 fans. The maker insisted that with 100 fans "our fan controller is not even breaking a sweat." Incidentally, the controller supports up to four integrated temperature probes to check if it is, actually, sweating.

Karanovic also sought to show the flexibility of his system by using wiring/splitters so that the first two headers controlled 50 fans each. If he'd had enough fans he could have theoretically expanded the cooling wall to 500 fans controlled by his OpenFan software in this way. But there are some other limits to the controller which means it tops out at around 200 fans.

In summary, this beastly cooling "contraption probably makes no sense," admitted the OpenFAN XL controller designer. However, he could have demonstrated it with some TrashBench-style shenanigans (or in an actual collab) by funneling a 100 fan-powered gust of air at a GPU, PC, laptop or so on.

Recent findings suggest that if you can think of a use for the OpenFan XL, you can make one yourself or grab one from Karanovic Research for $2,355, currently discounted from $2,926 on pre-order, by following the link in the intro. The product retail page more seriously pitches the controller as a useful product for server or other high-power device builders.
